session.question: How doeas sustainable marketing relate to enviromental sustainability in shaping a company"s image, and what kinds of consumption changes are described as ways to advance sufficiency transitions?
session.answer:
Sustainable marketing is linked to environmental sustainability in company image formation because it communicates that a firm is environmentally responsible and aligned with sustainability goals. In the cited studies, this improves brand image, builds customer trust, strengthens reputation, and can support loyalty and competitive advantage; in some cases, brand image mediates the effect of sustainability marketing on responsible consumer behavior. CSR (corporate social responsibility) can further strengthen these effects on brand image and related outcomes. (sujanska2023sustainablemarketingand chunk 1, jia2023promotingresponsiblesustainable chunk 1, gong2023howsustainablemarketing chunk 1)

Sufficiency transitions are advanced through four main consumption changes: absolute reductions in consumption, modal shifts to less resource-intensive options, product longevity, and sharing practices. These changes are discussed across housing, nutrition, mobility, and miscellaneous consumption, with the goal of reducing ecological footprints, especially among high-consuming groups. The review also identifies barriers such as consumer attitudes, culture, economic and political systems, and the physical environment, while noting that businesses, policymakers, citizens, NGOs, and educators can act as enabling agents. (sandberg2021sufficiencytransitionsa chunk 1)

session.context:
pqac-5d0464da: The article says sufficiency in sustainability research can involve four main kinds of consumption changes: absolute reductions in consumption, modal shifts to less resource-intensive options, product longevity (using products longer), and sharing practices. It reviews these sufficiency practices across housing, nutrition, mobility, and miscellaneous consumption, emphasizing that reducing ecological footprints may require substantial changes in consumption patterns, especially for high-consuming groups. It also notes that barriers and actors influence whether such sufficiency transitions can be advanced.
From Maria Sandberg. Sufficiency transitions: a review of consumption changes for environmental sustainability. Journal of Cleaner Production, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2021.126097, doi:10.1016/j.jclepro.2021.126097.

pqac-8c68d84c: The excerpt says sustainability has become an important part of a company’s image and brand identity because consumers are increasingly environmentally conscious. Firms that adopt sustainable practices and reduce environmental impact can show responsibility to society and the planet, which helps build customer trust and a positive reputation. The paper argues that sustainability in a company’s image can significantly affect corporate reputation, success, and long-term viability. It also notes that companies using eco-friendly and socially responsible practices are more likely to gain customer loyalty, competitive advantage, and stronger brand images. Thus, environmental sustainability is closely linked to how the firm is perceived and how reputable it is.
From Lucia Šujanská and Margaréta Nadányiová. Sustainable marketing and its impact on the image of the company. Marketing and Management of Innovations, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.21272/mmi.2023.2-06, doi:10.21272/mmi.2023.2-06.

pqac-37809334: The excerpt says sufficiency is an approach needed to halt environmental degradation and reduce ecological footprints, especially through changes in consumption patterns among high-consuming groups. In shaping a company’s image, sustainable marketing would be relevant because it signals environmental responsibility and alignment with sustainability goals. The article identifies four consumption changes that can advance sufficiency transitions: absolute reductions in consumption, modal shifts, product longevity, and sharing practices. It also notes examples across housing, nutrition, mobility, and miscellaneous consumption. Barriers include consumer attitudes, culture, the economic and political systems, and the physical environment, while actors such as businesses, policymakers, citizens, NGOs, and educators can help advance these changes.
From Maria Sandberg. Sufficiency transitions: a review of consumption changes for environmental sustainability. Journal of Cleaner Production, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2021.126097, doi:10.1016/j.jclepro.2021.126097.

pqac-612cb2fa: The excerpt reports that in this 2023 study on sustainability marketing in hotels, brand image is a key mediating mechanism: sustainability marketing improves brand image, which in turn promotes responsible sustainable consumer behavior. It also finds that corporate social responsibility (CSR) moderates this relationship, strengthening the effect of sustainability marketing on brand image at higher CSR levels. Although the excerpt does not directly discuss environmental sustainability or corporate reputation in general terms, it implies that a stronger brand image is part of how sustainability-related actions and CSR shape consumer perceptions and outcomes.
From Tong Jia, Shahid Iqbal, Arslan Ayub, Tehreem Fatima, and Zeeshan Rasool. Promoting responsible sustainable consumer behavior through sustainability marketing: the boundary effects of corporate social responsibility and brand image. Sustainability, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/su15076092, doi:10.3390/su15076092.

pqac-1787bf4c: The excerpt is about sustainable marketing and its effects on brand image, customer engagement, and sustainable purchase intention in the electric vehicle sector. It reports that sustainable marketing improves brand image, and that brand image in turn enhances customer engagement and sustainable purchase intentions. Corporate social responsibility (CSR) strengthens the relationship between brand image and both customer engagement and sustainable purchase intentions. However, the excerpt does not directly discuss how a firm’s image is linked specifically to environmental sustainability and corporate reputation beyond these brand-image effects.
From Yanping Gong, Jun Xiao, Xiuyuan Tang, and Jinglu Li. How sustainable marketing influences the customer engagement and sustainable purchase intention? the moderating role of corporate social responsibility. Frontiers in Psychology, 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1128686, doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1128686.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How doeas sustainable marketing relate to enviromental sustainability in shaping a company"s image, and what kinds of consumption changes are described as ways to advance sufficiency transitions?

Sustainable marketing is linked to environmental sustainability in company image formation because it communicates that a firm is environmentally responsible and aligned with sustainability goals. In the cited studies, this improves brand image, builds customer trust, strengthens reputation, and can support loyalty and competitive advantage; in some cases, brand image mediates the effect of sustainability marketing on responsible consumer behavior. CSR (corporate social responsibility) can further strengthen these effects on brand image and related outcomes. (sujanska2023sustainablemarketingand chunk 1, jia2023promotingresponsiblesustainable chunk 1, gong2023howsustainablemarketing chunk 1)

Sufficiency transitions are advanced through four main consumption changes: absolute reductions in consumption, modal shifts to less resource-intensive options, product longevity, and sharing practices. These changes are discussed across housing, nutrition, mobility, and miscellaneous consumption, with the goal of reducing ecological footprints, especially among high-consuming groups. The review also identifies barriers such as consumer attitudes, culture, economic and political systems, and the physical environment, while noting that businesses, policymakers, citizens, NGOs, and educators can act as enabling agents. (sandberg2021sufficiencytransitionsa chunk 1)
